evidence: Quint. 1.5.47: per tempora, ut in verbō … peccātur
terms.comment: The word for time is the word for tense, and the tenses are named with an adjective: tempus praesēns, praeteritum, futūrum. The question is Cujus temporis est?, what tense is it? (Traupman 241); in the present tense, tempore praesentī (227).

phrases.latin: in participiō per genus et cāsum, ut in vocābulō, per tempora, ut in verbō, per numerum, ut in utrōque, peccātur
phrases.english: in the participle one goes wrong in gender and case, as in a noun, in tense, as in a verb, and in number, as in both
What tense is it? — The present.

phrases.latin: quaedam verba etiam mūtantur, ut ferō in praeteritō
phrases.english: some verbs even change, as ferō does in the past tense

sources: Quintilian checked against the Perseus Latin texts, and cited by its numbering.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 226, 227, 241, 249, 357, 358, 361, 364.
